teaching.task: Explain how named fungal reproductive cells form; classify supplied pathways using mechanism evidence.
teaching.causalExplanation: DNA copying and nuclear division supply the bud with inherited information. Dispersal gives spores new locations, while suitable conditions permit germination. Nuclear fusion joins chromosome sets; meiosis reduces them. Spore production alone is insufficient classification evidence.

scenes.narrationCue: Imagine finding a fungal spore on a surface. Can you tell whether it came from sexual or asexual reproduction? The spore alone does not settle that question. Fungi can produce spores through either pathway. We need to know how it was formed. Today we will use two named examples to explain that difference: budding in baker's yeast, and asexual spores in bread mould. Then we will connect yeast spores to a sexual cycle.

scenes.narrationCue: Baker's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, is a single-celled fungus. In budding, a small outgrowth develops on the parent cell. The cell copies its DNA, the information it passes on. Its nucleus, the compartment containing that DNA, divides by mitosis. Mitosis separates copied genetic information into two nuclei. One nucleus enters the growing bud. The bud can then separate as a daughter cell. This event is asexual because no reproductive cells or nuclei fuse. Copying supports similar inherited information, although mutations, changes in DNA, can still occur.

scenes.narrationCue: Now consider the asexual pathway of bread mould, Rhizopus stolonifer. Its body includes hyphae: thin growing threads. A sporangium is a spore-containing structure at the tip of a specialised stalk. In this pathway, spores form through mitosis without fusion. Releasing them allows dispersal, movement away from the parent fungus. A spore that reaches suitable conditions can germinate, meaning it begins to grow. It produces hyphae that develop into a new fungal body. Dispersal creates opportunities, but landing somewhere does not guarantee growth. The spore still needs suitable moisture, nutrients and other conditions.

scenes.narrationCue: The same yeast species has another pathway. In a simplified baker's yeast model, compatible cells of different mating types can join. Their nuclei then fuse, bringing chromosome sets together. A chromosome is a DNA-containing structure. A haploid cell has one set of chromosomes; a diploid cell has two. Nuclear fusion produces a diploid cell. This is part of sexual reproduction. Compatibility matters: simply putting any two yeast cells together does not establish that fusion will occur. Fungi do not all use the sperm-and-egg arrangement we met in animals and flowering plants.

scenes.narrationCue: Under suitable nutrient-limiting conditions, a diploid baker's yeast cell can undergo meiosis and form spores. Meiosis is a cell division that reduces two chromosome sets to one and can reshuffle inherited information. The resulting haploid nuclei are packaged into spores. This spore formation belongs to the sexual life cycle we have just traced: fusion brought sets together, and meiosis separates them again. It is different from the mitotic spores in our bread-mould example. So the word spore describes a reproductive cell, not a guarantee that the pathway was asexual. These are selected examples, not a rule that all fungi have the same life cycle.

scenes.narrationCue: Case A is asexual. The supplied mitosis-and-no-fusion evidence explains that classification. Case B traces a sexual pathway: compatible cells and nuclei fuse, followed later by meiosis and spore formation. Both cases end with spores, but they reach that result differently. If you classified both as asexual just because spores were named, return to the events that produced them. No observation about the final shape can replace that pathway evidence.

scenes.narrationCue: When you meet a fungal reproductive event, ask how the new cell was formed. Budding in our yeast example grows a daughter cell without fusion. Our bread-mould example makes mitotic spores. Yeast can also form spores within a sexual cycle involving nuclear fusion and meiosis. Keep those examples scoped to their organisms and supplied conditions. Next we will consider bacteria, where cell division and exchanges of DNA need to be distinguished. You can pause the optional notes screen to record the essentials.
